subject: Anatomy
summary: The thyroid is a butterfly‑shaped endocrine organ in the anterior neck that makes T3/T4 hormones controlling metabolism. Its location, blood supply and nerve relations are key to interpreting neck masses and surgical risk.

sections.p: A paired, lobed organ lying in the lower neck, anterior to the trachea. It stores and releases thyroid hormones that regulate basal metabolic rate, heart rate and growth.
b: Two lobes connected by an isthmus
Enlarges in goitre, inflammation, or tumour

sections.p: The gland spans C5–T1, with each lobe extending laterally from the midline. The isthmus overlies the second and third tracheal rings. Histologically it has follicles filled with colloid.
b: Parathyroids sit on the posterior surface

sections.p: Anteriorly the skin and strap muscles; posteriorly the trachea, oesophagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves; laterally the carotid sheaths.
b: Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the groove between thyroid and trachea
Superior thyroid artery lies just above the isthmus

sections.p: Arises from the superior thyroid artery (branch of external carotid) and inferior thyroid artery (branch of thyrocervical trunk). Venous drainage follows the superior, middle and inferior thyroid veins to the internal jugular.
b: Bleeding is a common intra‑operative hazard

sections.p: Sympathetic fibers travel with the superior thyroid artery; parasympathetic input is minimal. The recurrent laryngeal nerves provide motor innervation to the vocal cords and are at risk during surgery.
b: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve controls pitch

sections.p: Synthesises thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) from iodine and tyrosine. Release is controlled by TSH from the pituitary, itself regulated by TRH from the hypothalamus.
b: T4 is a pro‑hormone, converted peripherally to active T3
Feedback loop keeps hormone levels within narrow limits

sections.p: Enlargement (goitre) may be diffuse or nodular; inflammation (thyroiditis) releases stored hormone causing transient hyperthyroidism; neoplasia can be benign (adenoma) or malignant (carcinoma).
b: Diffuse goitre: iodine deficiency, Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis
Nodular goitre: multinodular disease, cysts, carcinoma
Thyroiditis: viral, post‑partum, autoimmune (Hashimoto) – painful or painless

t.b: Is the gland over‑ or under‑producing hormone? Low TSH = hyperthyroidism, high TSH = hypothyroidism
Quantifies active hormone levels; helps differentiate subclinical from overt disease
Detects nodule size, composition, calcifications; guides fine‑needle aspiration. If unavailable, rely on palpation and clinical risk factors
Answers whether a nodule is benign or malignant; essential before surgery

sections.p: On inspection look for neck swelling, skin changes, or stridor. Palpate for size, consistency, tenderness, and assess for bruit (suggests Graves). Auscultate for thrill.
b: A midline, smooth, non‑tender goitre often indicates iodine deficiency
A firm, irregular nodule raises suspicion for carcinoma
Hoarseness after thyroid surgery suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden airway obstruction from a rapidly expanding thyroid mass
Severe hyperthyroid storm (fever, tachycardia, altered mental status)
Rapidly enlarging painful thyroid with fever (possible abscess)

faq.q: Why does iodine deficiency cause a goitre?
faq.a: Low iodine limits hormone synthesis, prompting TSH‑driven thyroid growth to capture more iodine.

faq.q: What clinical sign suggests Graves disease?
faq.a: A diffuse, smooth goitre with a palpable thrill or audible bruit.
For compressive symptoms, suspicious cytology, or confirmed carcinoma.

exam: Describe the arterial supply of the thyroid and why injury to the inferior thyroid artery is significant during surgery.
Explain the feedback loop controlling TSH, T4, and T3, and how it is altered in primary hyperthyroidism.
List three common causes of a diffuse goitre and one key clinical feature that helps differentiate each.
